title: UK Picks Portugal's Tekever for £400M Drone Deal as Germany Surges Arms Exports to Israel
subhead: Britain's Ministry of Defence selected Portugal-based Tekever to supply the British Army's new CORVUS surveillance drone under a deal worth up to £400 million, replacing the aging Watchkeeper fleet amid a broader push in European defense procurement.

sections.heading: UK Taps Portuguese Maker for £400M Army Drone Replacement
sections.body:
The UK Ministry of Defence has selected Tekever, the Lisbon-based maker of AI-enabled autonomous systems, to deliver CORVUS, the British Army's new surveillance capability, in a contract worth up to £400 million over ten years, according to sUAS News. The program replaces the Army's Watchkeeper fleet with Tekever's battle-proven AR5 platform, which carries up to 50 kg of surveillance payloads including cameras and sensors for round-the-clock intelligence gathering. FlightGlobal reports deliveries are expected to begin before year-end.

The program will sustain and create hundreds of jobs across Tekever's UK sites in the South West and Wales, supported by a supply chain of UK small and medium enterprises. Tekever emphasized CORVUS will enable 'full UK sovereign control' over capability evolution, letting battlefield lessons and emerging technologies be integrated continuously. The award marks a notable EU supplier win in a British Army program at a moment of heightened UK defense spending.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's drone-makers are breaking into national replacement programs beyond their home markets, and the UK — a top-tier buyer — has handed a flagship surveillance contract to a Portuguese firm, signaling that sovereign-control guarantees weigh as heavily as domestic sourcing in the new procurement climate.

sections.heading: Germany's Arms Exports to Israel Surge, Final Dolphin Submarine Delivered
sections.body:
Germany has approved nearly €800 million — roughly $930 million — in military export licenses to Israel in the past six months, with a particular focus on a submarine project, according to Anadolu Agency and Globes. The surge runs alongside the delivery of Israel's newest submarine capability: shipbuilder thyssenkrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) has shipped the third and final Advanced Dolphin-class submarine to the Israeli Navy, The Defense Post reports, completing a class whose lead boat, the INS Drakon, was the largest conventional submarine ever built for Israel.

The deliveries come as Germany has faced legal and political pressure over arms sales to Israel. The export licenses' submarine focus points to the naval-deterrence dimension of the relationship: Fox News framed Israel's new German-built boat, valued around $634 million, as a major boost to deterrence against Iran. The approvals illustrate how, despite periodic court challenges and diplomatic friction, Berlin's defense-industrial ties with Israel remain operationally deep.
sections.whyItMatters: The submarine-and-arms flow reveals the concrete industrial backbone of the Germany-Israel relationship, which has been obscured by public debate over export bans. The final Dolphin delivery closes out a two-decade program and locks in German shipbuilding as Israel's naval-deterrence supplier.

sections.heading: Canada's GCAP Observer Status Opens Business Lane for Firms Like CAE
sections.body:
Canada formally joined the British-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) as its first observer country, announced at the Farnborough Airshow on July 21, per Reuters and SCMP. Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty signed alongside UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, Italy's Guido Crosetto and Japan's Shinjiro Koizumi. The observer status marks GCAP's first expansion beyond its three founding members since the sixth-generation fighter program launched in December 2022, with a targeted in-service date around 2035.

SCMP frames the move as Ottawa diversifying its defense partnerships amid US-China competition in future air power. For Canada's defense industrial base, the status opens a lane for companies to compete for work — CAE, the Montreal-based simulation giant, is already assessing the business opportunity from Canada's new position, according to Breaking Defense. The wider context, Reuters notes, is a push by European and partner militaries to reduce reliance on US weapons and technology.
sections.whyItMatters: GCAP's first expansion is less about a new aircraft order than about widening the industrial tent: observer status lets allied firms position for future work packages, and Canada's move shows middle powers hedging their air-power futures beyond US platforms.

sections.heading: Congress Locks In $500M Taiwan Defense Money as Trump Holds $14B Package
sections.body:
The US House of Representatives has passed a bill including $500 million in Foreign Military Financing for Taiwan in the FY2027 appropriations process, Defense News reports, even as President Trump continues to hold back approval of a larger $14 billion weapons package for Taiwan. Trump pulled the larger package back in May after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Defense News analysts note the half-billion-dollar allocation does not commit funds to a specific arms package — Foreign Military Financing covers how weapons are funded rather than which systems are transferred — but it signals Congress has not eased security support for Taiwan despite the Trump-Xi detente. Huang Chung-ting, an associate research fellow at Taipei's Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said the funding 'demonstrates that Congress has not reduced its security support for Taiwan following the Trump-Xi meeting.' The tension leaves Taiwan's near-term arms pipeline split between congressional intent and White House hesitation.
sections.whyItMatters: The split between a Congress willing to fund Taiwan and a White House holding back a major package is the crux of Washington's Taiwan policy wobble: financing flows can be appropriated, but actual transfers and Trump's posture remain the gating variable.

sections.heading: Iran Says It Won't Seek Talks as Hormuz War Drags Into Pause
sections.body:
In the ongoing US-Iran conflict — now approaching five months — Iran has claimed control of the Strait of Hormuz and said it is not seeking talks after the US bombing halt, per Reuters, even as oil prices plunged 7-9 percent on de-escalation hopes in the markets (NBC News, BBC). A parallel effort to reopen the strait is stalling: Iran-Oman talks with Gulf states on 'new Hormuz routes' have been postponed with no date set, according to Moneycontrol and the Khaleej Times. Trump, for his part, rejected talks while claiming 'total control' of Hormuz after US strikes, per MSN.

Separately, SCMP highlights a strategic friction point: Trump's Iran strikes have damaged the US strategy to contain China via the Chabahar port, a key Iranian port that serves India's and China's trade routes into Central Asia, complicating the Indo-Pacific posture the strikes were partly meant to protect.
sections.whyItMatters: Markets are pricing peace, but Tehran's insistence that it is not seeking talks and the stalled Oman-mediated track suggest the de-escalation window may be narrower than oil traders assume — while the war's side effects are already undermining Washington's broader China-containment strategy.

sections.heading: Canada and Ukraine Deepen Joint Drone and Defense Production
sections.body:
Canada and Ukraine have agreed to jointly produce defense technology, including ramping up drone production and building out Canada's defense industrial base, under what Ottawa calls a '100-year partnership', according to Breaking Defense and the Prime Minister's Office. Canada has also selected six systems in its broader domestic drone push while expanding ties with Ukraine, Aerotime reports. The pact extends the Western pattern of co-production with Ukraine that has emerged during the conflict, moving beyond transfers toward shared manufacturing.

The arrangement pairs Ukraine's battlefield-proven drone know-how with Canadian industrial capacity, part of a wider trend in which allied states are using wartime lessons to build resilient, domestic unmanned-systems supply chains rather than relying on a few dominant producers.
sections.whyItMatters: The Canada-Ukraine co-production model is a template for how mid-tier allies are industrializing drone tech learned in combat: shared manufacturing ties defense relationships to actual capability rather than just aid packages.

bottomLine: Today's defense industry picture is defined by European procurement momentum rather than the Iran war: the UK handed its flagship Army surveillance-drone contract to Portugal's Tekever in a £400M deal, Germany surged nearly $930M in arms export licenses to Israel focused on a submarine project as the final Advanced Dolphin boat was delivered, and Canada joined GCAP as an observer, opening business lanes for firms like CAE. In parallel, US-China competition sharpened — Congress funded $500M for Taiwan while the White House holds a $14B package, and the Iran conflict's fallout is complicating Washington's Chabahar-based containment of China. The thread running through each is a rebalancing of defense-industrial ties away from singular reliance on US platforms and toward diversified, sovereign-control-oriented supply chains.
sources: sUAS News, FlightGlobal, Reuters, SCMP, Defense News, Breaking Defense, Anadolu Agency, The Defense Post, Fox News, MSN, Yahoo/AOL, Moneycontrol, Khaleej Times, NBC News, BBC, Aerotime, Globes, PressTV, Palestine Chronicle, army-technology
